topic: Automate, delegate or delete? A 3-question filter
hook: Automate it, delegate it, or delete it?
takeaway: Before automating a task, check that it should exist and that its steps are fixed.
cta: Save it and run your own to-do list through it.
image_text:
Automate it, delegate it, or delete it?
Ask these 3 questions before you build anything.
1. Does this task need to happen at all? No → DELETE it.
2. Are the steps the same every time? No → a person does it.
3. Does it happen every week or more? Yes → AUTOMATE it.
Automation makes a good process faster. It makes a bad process fail faster.
caption:
Before you automate anything, ask if it should exist at all.

The 3-question filter I'd use before building any workflow:
1. Does this task need to happen? If not, delete it.
2. Are the steps the same every time? If not, a person should do it (or write the rules first).
3. Does it happen every week or more? Then automation pays back the setup time.

Automating a messy process just makes the mess faster.

Run your to-do list through it this week. You might delete a task before you automate one.

Agent: AI that can do things (search, send, update a sheet) instead of only replying.

topic: Prompt rescue: 6 follow-ups when the first answer is bad

cta: Save it for the next disappointing answer.
image_text:
Bad AI answer? Don't start over. Send one of these.
Too generic → “Use my details: [paste facts].”
Too long → “Cut to 5 lines. Keep the numbers.”
Wrong tone → “Rewrite like I'm texting a respected client.”
Not sure it's true → “Which parts are you unsure about?”
Messy → “Make a table: step, owner, deadline.”
Missed the point → “My goal is [X]. What would you change?”
caption:
Most people give up on a bad AI answer and open a new chat. The second message is usually where the good answer comes from.

Match the problem to the fix:
Too generic → “Use my details: [paste facts].”
Too long → “Cut to 5 lines. Keep the numbers.”
Wrong tone → “Rewrite like I'm texting a respected client.”
Not sure it's true → “Which parts are you unsure about?”
Messy → “Make a table: step, owner, deadline.”
Missed the point → “My goal is [X]. What would you change?”

Next time an answer disappoints you, send one of these before you give up on the chat.

topic: Why AI makes things up (and the one prompt that catches it)
hook: AI gave me a source. It doesn't exist.
takeaway: AI predicts likely words, so ask it to quote the exact line behind every claim.
cta: Follow for more AI Myth Checks.
script_text:
[0-3 s] VO: AI gave me a source. It doesn't exist. | TEXT: A source that doesn't exist | SHOW: Asif holding his phone: an AI answer with a neat book citation; quick cut to an empty search result.
[3-7 s] VO: It wasn't lying. It predicts the next likely word. | TEXT: It predicts the next word | SHOW: Animation: a sentence builds word by word with small probability bars.
[7-12.5 s] VO: Ask for a source it doesn't have, and it predicts what a source looks like. | TEXT: predicts what a source LOOKS like | SHOW: A citation assembles: author → title → year → page.
[12.5-16 s] VO: Real-looking author. Real-looking title. Doesn't exist. | TEXT: looks real ≠ is real | SHOW: Search result page → 'NOT FOUND' stamp.
[16-20 s] VO: That's a hallucination. Confident, fluent, and wrong. | TEXT: Hallucination = confident + wrong | SHOW: Label slides in; Asif points at it.
[20-25 s] VO: It happens most with exact numbers, dates, quotes, links and laws. | TEXT: numbers · dates · quotes · links · laws | SHOW: Five icons pop in sequence.
[25-30 s] VO: The fix: turn on web search, or give it your own document. | TEXT: Fix: search ON or give it the source | SHOW: Screen recording: toggling search; uploading a PDF.
[30-35 s] VO: Then ask: “Quote the exact line you used for each claim.” | TEXT: “Quote the exact line for each claim.” | SHOW: Typed prompt; answer shows quoted lines highlighted.
[35-40 s] VO: No quote, no trust. Follow for more AI myth checks. | TEXT: No quote = no trust | SHOW: Asif to camera; series tag 'AI Myth Check'.
caption:
AI gave me a perfect-looking source. It doesn't exist.

Language models generate the most likely next words. Ask for a source they don't have, and they can generate something that looks like a source: real-looking author, real-looking title, doesn't exist. That's a hallucination.

Highest risk: exact numbers, dates, quotes, links and laws.

The check I use:
1. Turn on web search, or upload the document yourself.
2. Ask: “Quote the exact line you used for each claim.”
No quote, no trust.

Learn n8n in 4 words
Trigger: what starts the workflow (new message, form, schedule).
Node: one step. Read, decide, write or send.
Credential: your saved login to an app, kept separate from the steps.
Execution: one run of the workflow, with a log of every step.

Trigger: what starts the workflow: a new message, a form, a time of day.
Node: one step: read data, decide, write, send.
Credential: your saved login to an app. Keep keys and passwords here, never typed inside a node.
Execution: one run of the workflow. Open it to see exactly what happened at each step.

topic: 5 hot spots where AI answers go wrong
hook: Check these 5 things in every AI answer
takeaway: AI mistakes cluster in numbers, dates, names and quotes, links, and laws, so check those first.
cta: Save it next to your AI app.
image_text:
Check these 5 things in every AI answer
Numbers: prices, percentages, totals. Recalculate.
Dates: 'latest', 'this year', deadlines.
Names & quotes: real person? Real words?
Links & sources: click them. Some don't exist.
Laws & rules: they differ by country. Ask a local expert.
Use AI answers as a first draft, not the final word.
caption:
AI mistakes aren't random. They show up in the same 5 places.

✔ Numbers: recalculate prices, percentages and totals.
✔ Dates: “latest” and “this year” are often out of date.
✔ Names & quotes: check the person exists and said it.
✔ Links & sources: click them. Some are invented.
✔ Laws & rules: they change by country. Ask someone local.

Use AI answers as a first draft, not the final word.

cta: Message 'AUTOMATE' with a voice note describing the task.
script_text:
[0-3 s] VO: What do you repeat every single day? | TEXT: What do you repeat daily? | SHOW: Asif, tight close-up.
[3-7.5 s] VO: Copying orders. Answering the same questions. Making the same report. | TEXT: orders · questions · reports | SHOW: Montage of this month's Reels (own footage).
[7.5-12.5 s] VO: This month I showed you how many of those can run without you. | TEXT: 30 days of builds | SHOW: Montage continues.
[12.5-17 s] VO: Now I want to hear yours. | TEXT: Your turn | SHOW: Asif to camera.
[17-22 s] VO: Message me the word AUTOMATE, and describe the task in one voice note. | TEXT: Message: AUTOMATE + voice note | SHOW: Messenger icon; voice-note animation.
[22-27.5 s] VO: I'll reply myself, ask three questions, and tell you honestly if it's worth it. | TEXT: I reply · 3 questions · honest answer | SHOW: Asif to camera.
[27.5-32 s] VO: Sometimes the answer is no. A template is enough. That's fine too. | TEXT: Sometimes: no. That's fine. | SHOW: Asif smiles.
[32-36 s] VO: So, before you scroll away, tell me: | TEXT:  | SHOW: Back to the frame-1 close-up (loop).
caption:
What do you repeat every single day? Copying orders, answering the same questions, building the same report?

This month I showed you how many of those can run without you. Now I want to hear yours.

Message me “AUTOMATE” and describe the task in one voice note. I'll reply myself, ask 3 questions, and tell you honestly if it's worth automating.

Sometimes the answer is no. A saved reply or a template is enough. That's fine too.
